text.p: LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault has proposed a merger of LVMH's wine and spirits business with those of Guinness and Grand Metropolitan in a quoted company, LVMH said on Wednesday.

It said in a statement that Arnault put the proposal to the chairmen of Guinness and Grand Met at a meeting in Paris on Wednesday. He said such a deal appeared to offer greater shareholder value than the proposed Grand Met-Guinness merger.

"LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, the largest shareholder in Guinness and Grand Met, offered a solution through the merger of the wine and spirits activities of Moet Hennessy, Guinness and Grand Met in an independent company listed on the stock exchange," LVMH said in the statement issued after a one-hour meeting between the three chairmen.

"Arnault asked the Guinness and Grand Met representatives to study this solution which seems to him will create significantly greater value for the shareholders of the three companies than the merger proposed by Guinness and Grand Met, both in terms of potential synergies and market valuation of a coherent company with a portfolio of prestige brands, clearly a leader in its market," the statement said.

Moet Hennessy, LVMH's drinks subsidiary in which Guinness holds 34 percent, makes Moet & Chandon and Pommery champagnes and Hennessy cognacs. Guinness labels include Johnny Walker and Dewar's whiskies and Gordon's Gin and Grand Met's brands include Smirnoff, J&B and Baileys.
LVMH said Grand Met chairman George Bull and Guinness chairman Tony Greener agreed to study proposals which Arnault would send to them quickly.
The British chairmen said in a separate statement issued after the meeting that they were open to Arnault's proposals.

"We have made it clear to Mr Arnault that we are, of course, open to any proposals provided that they create additional value for our shareholders beyond our existing proposal and that this is fairly shared between them," they said in a joint statement.
The meeting in Paris followed a two-pronged assault by Arnault on the British companies, which announced their planned 24 billion pound ($40 billion) merger on May 12.
Last month LVMH spent more than eight billion francs ($1.4 billion) to buy 6.4 percent of Grand Met in an apparent bid to line up enough votes to block the merger and force a hearing of his proposal.

LVMH had previously taken legal action against Guinness, in which it holds 14.2 percent, to force the company to sell its stakes in their valuable joint distribution ventures, which own the rights for 10 years to market Guinness brands in France, the United States and much of the Far East.
-- Christine Tierney, Paris Newsroom, +33 1 4221 5452 ($ = 0.602 British Pounds) ($ = 5.897 French Francs)
